question: What is JPA and what problem does it solve?
title: Java Persistence API (JPA) Explained
direct_answer: **JPA (Java Persistence API)** is a specification that defines how Java objects map to relational database tables. It solves the **object-relational impedance mismatch** — the gap between OOP concepts (inheritance, associations) and relational DB concepts (tables, foreign keys). Hibernate is the most common JPA implementation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of what JPA is vs JDBC and when to use it
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the impedance mismatch clearly and why ORM was invented

sections.title: JPA: Specification, Not Implementation
sections.content:
**JPA** is a Java EE/Jakarta EE specification (set of interfaces and rules) for ORM. You write code against JPA APIs (`EntityManager`, `@Entity`, `@Id`) and JPA providers (Hibernate, EclipseLink, OpenJPA) implement those APIs. This means your code works with any JPA provider.

**The problem JPA solves**: JDBC requires you to manually write SQL, map ResultSets to objects, handle relationships, and manage transactions. JPA handles all of this — you work with Java objects, and the framework generates and executes the SQL.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- JPA is a **specification** (`javax.persistence`/`jakarta.persistence` package)
- **Hibernate** is the most popular JPA implementation
- Spring Data JPA builds on top of JPA/Hibernate
- Main JPA concepts: `@Entity`, `@Id`, `EntityManager`, JPQL
- JPA handles: SQL generation, ResultSet mapping, relationship loading, caching
- Before JPA: JDBC with manual SQL and mapping (Spring JDBC Template)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: JPA stands for Java Persistence API, and it's a specification — a set of rules and interfaces — for mapping Java objects to relational database tables. The problem it solves is what's called the object-relational impedance mismatch: in Java we work with objects, inheritance, and collections, but databases think in terms of tables, rows, and foreign keys. Without JPA, you'd write JDBC code with raw SQL, manually map ResultSets to your objects, and handle relationships yourself. JPA abstracts all that away — you annotate your Java class with `@Entity`, and the framework handles generating SQL and mapping results. Hibernate is the most popular implementation of the JPA specification.

sections.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with Hibernate and PostgreSQL
sections.hook: JPA isn't a library you install — it's a contract that libraries like Hibernate agree to follow.

beats.heading: What it is
beats.body: JPA stands for Java Persistence API. It's a specification — a set of interfaces and rules published by Jakarta EE. You write code against those interfaces, and a provider like Hibernate does the actual work. Think of it like JDBC: JDBC is the spec, your database driver is the implementation.

beats.heading: Why it exists
beats.body: Before JPA, you wrote JDBC code: raw SQL strings, manual ResultSet loops, and hand-mapping each column to an object field. The gap between Java's object world and the database's table world is called the object-relational impedance mismatch. JPA was invented to close that gap.

beats.heading: What JPA handles for you
items: SQL generation from your annotated classes
Mapping query results back to Java objects
Loading related entities across foreign keys
A first-level cache to avoid redundant queries

beats.heading: Sharp edge
beats.body: sharp edge: JPA and Hibernate are not the same thing. JPA is the spec in the jakarta.persistence package. Hibernate is one implementation of that spec. Spring Data JPA is a layer on top that adds repositories and query generation. Interviewers love to test this distinction.

sections.cap: If you annotate a class with @Entity and add an @Id field, JPA knows everything it needs to generate the table mapping. Hibernate does the SQL; you just work with Java objects.
followup_handoff: Next natural question is usually how JPA compares to plain JDBC.
They may also ask you to name the core JPA annotations like @Entity, @Id, and @GeneratedValue.

followup_questions: What is the difference between JPA and Hibernate?
What is the difference between JPA and JDBC?

question: What is the difference between JPA and JDBC?
title: JPA vs JDBC — Key Differences
direct_answer: **JDBC** is a low-level API for executing raw SQL against a database — you write SQL strings and manually map `ResultSet` to objects. **JPA** is a high-level ORM specification that generates SQL from Java objects. JPA is more productive; JDBC gives more control and is faster for complex queries.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying JPA is always better — JDBC is preferred for complex bulk operations
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Acknowledge when each is appropriate — JPA for CRUD, JDBC for complex queries

rows: Overhead for simple cases, smart for complex

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: JDBC and JPA operate at different levels. JDBC is the foundation — you write SQL strings like `SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?`, execute them, and manually map each column of the `ResultSet` to your Java object's fields. JPA sits on top and automates that. You annotate your `User` class with `@Entity` and Hibernate figures out the table structure, generates the SELECT statement, and maps the results. JPA is more productive for standard CRUD operations. The tradeoff is that for complex reporting queries, batch operations, or performance-critical paths, JDBC or native SQL gives you more control. In Spring Boot, you can use both in the same application — JPA for most things, JDBC Template for the complex ones.

sections.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with Hibernate and PostgreSQL
sections.hook: JDBC is a hammer; JPA is a power drill. Pick based on the job, not the hype.

beats.heading: What each is
beats.body: JDBC is Java's low-level database API. You write a SQL string, hand it to a connection, and loop over the ResultSet row by row to build your object. JPA is a higher-level ORM spec. You annotate a class with @Entity and let Hibernate generate the SQL for you.

beats.heading: When to pick each
beats.body: Use JPA for everyday save, find, update, and delete operations — it's faster to write and easier to read. Switch to JDBC or native queries for bulk inserts, reporting queries with many joins, or cases where you need exact SQL control for performance tuning.

beats.heading: Non-obvious
beats.body: non-obvious: you don't have to choose one. Spring Boot lets you use JPA repositories for most operations and inject a JdbcTemplate for the complex ones. Many production apps do exactly this.

sections.cap: JPA trades SQL control for productivity. For standard CRUD that trade is always worth it. For complex reporting or bulk loads, drop down to JDBC. Using both in one app is completely normal.
followup_handoff: They'll often follow up by asking when you'd choose native SQL over JPQL.
You might also get asked whether Spring JdbcTemplate is the same as JDBC — it's a thin wrapper, not JPA.

followup_questions: When would you choose JDBC over JPA?
Can you mix JPA and JDBC in the same Spring Boot application?

question: What is EntityManager in JPA and what operations does it provide?
title: EntityManager in JPA Explained
direct_answer: **`EntityManager`** is the core JPA API for managing entity lifecycle. Key operations: `persist()` (insert), `find()` (select by PK), `merge()` (update), `remove()` (delete), `createQuery()` (JPQL queries). It represents one unit of work and manages the first-level cache.

interviewer_intent.testing: JPA API knowledge beyond Spring Data abstraction
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing EntityManager exists because Spring Data JPA hides it
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that Spring Data JPA repositories use EntityManager internally

sections.title: EntityManager Operations
Key Points
sections.content:
- `persist(entity)` — INSERT (entity must be in 'new' state)
- `find(Class, id)` — SELECT by primary key
- `merge(entity)` — UPDATE (entity may be detached)
- `remove(entity)` — DELETE
- `createQuery(jpql)` — run JPQL (SQL-like but against entities)
- `flush()` — sync persistence context to DB
- `@PersistenceContext` — inject EntityManager
- Spring Data JPA repos use EntityManager internally

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: `EntityManager` is JPA's main interface for database operations. It's what actually talks to the database. The key methods are `persist()` to insert, `find()` to look up by primary key, `merge()` to update a detached entity, and `remove()` to delete. For queries, you use `createQuery()` with JPQL — that's a SQL-like language that works against entity classes instead of table names. In Spring Boot with Spring Data JPA, you rarely use `EntityManager` directly because the repository interfaces abstract it away. But Spring Data JPA's generated methods all delegate to `EntityManager` under the hood, so it's important to know it exists.

sections.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with Hibernate and PostgreSQL
sections.hook: EntityManager is the real engine behind every Spring Data JPA repository method you've ever called.

beats.heading: What it is
beats.body: EntityManager is the core JPA interface for database operations. Every entity you load, save, update, or delete goes through an EntityManager. When you use Spring Data JPA repositories, they're backed by an EntityManager — it's just hidden behind the interface.

beats.heading: The five key operations
items: persist(entity) — INSERT a new entity into the database
find(User.class, id) — SELECT by primary key

beats.heading: How you use it
beats.body: You inject EntityManager with @PersistenceContext and call its methods inside a @Transactional method. One EntityManager represents one unit of work — it holds the first-level cache for that transaction.

beats.heading: Candidates miss
beats.body: candidates miss: Spring Data JPA's save(), findById(), and deleteById() are convenience methods that call persist(), find(), and remove() on the EntityManager internally. Knowing this helps you debug lazy loading and transaction boundary issues that the repository abstraction can hide.

sections.cap: EntityManager is what JPA actually runs on. Spring Data JPA just generates the method calls so you don't have to write them yourself.
followup_handoff: They'll likely ask about the persistence context next, since EntityManager manages it.
Expect a follow-up on the difference between persist() and merge() — it trips up a lot of candidates.

followup_questions: What is JPQL and how does it differ from SQL?
What is the difference between persist() and merge()?

question: What is JPQL and how is it different from SQL?
title: JPQL vs SQL in JPA
direct_answer: **JPQL (Java Persistence Query Language)** queries entity classes and their fields, not database tables and columns. `SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.name = :name` queries the `User` entity class. It's database-agnostic — the JPA provider translates it to the correct dialect SQL.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing table names instead of entity class names in JPQL
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the database portability benefit — same JPQL works on MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle

rows: SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.name = :name

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: JPQL is SQL-like but it operates on your Java entity classes instead of database tables. So instead of writing `SELECT * FROM users`, you write `SELECT u FROM User u` where `User` is your Java class name. And instead of column names, you use field names from your class. The main advantage over raw SQL is that JPQL is database-agnostic — you write it once and Hibernate translates it to the correct SQL dialect for MySQL, PostgreSQL, or Oracle. JPQL also lets you navigate object relationships naturally — instead of explicit JOINs, you write `u.orders` to navigate the relationship. For complex native SQL that can't be expressed in JPQL, you can use `@Query(value="...", nativeQuery=true)` in Spring Data.

sections.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with Hibernate and PostgreSQL
sections.hook: JPQL looks like SQL but talks to your Java classes, not your database tables.

beats.heading: What each is
beats.body: SQL queries tables. You write SELECT * FROM users WHERE user_name = 'alice'. JPQL queries entity classes. You write SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.name = 'alice' — User is your Java class, and name is a field on it.

beats.heading: The portability win
beats.body: The big advantage is that JPQL is database-agnostic. You write one query and Hibernate generates the correct SQL for MySQL, PostgreSQL, or Oracle at runtime. This means switching databases only requires a config change, not rewriting queries.

beats.heading: Gotcha
beats.body: gotcha: the most common JPQL mistake is using the table name instead of the entity class name. If your class is User but your table is tbl_users, your JPQL must say FROM User, not FROM tbl_users. JPQL never sees table names.

sections.cap: Use JPQL when your query maps naturally to your entity model. Use nativeQuery=true on @Query only when you need database-specific SQL features that JPQL can't express.
followup_handoff: They'll often ask when you'd use native SQL over JPQL — think database-specific functions or bulk updates.
Spring Data's @Query annotation uses JPQL by default, so that's a natural follow-up topic.

followup_questions: When would you use native SQL over JPQL?
How do you use @Query in Spring Data JPA?
What is the Criteria API in JPA?

question: What is the persistence context in JPA?
title: JPA Persistence Context Explained
direct_answer: The **persistence context** is a set of managed entity instances within a transaction. It acts as a first-level cache — if you load the same entity twice by ID, JPA returns the same Java object. Changes to managed entities are automatically detected and flushed to the database on transaction commit.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing persistence context (first-level cache) with second-level cache
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain dirty checking — you don't need to call save() after modifying a managed entity

sections.title: How Persistence Context Works
sections.content:
The persistence context is the **first-level cache** — an in-memory store of entities loaded in the current transaction. When you call `em.find(User.class, 1L)` twice in the same transaction, JPA returns the same Java object without hitting the database the second time.

**Dirty checking**: JPA tracks changes to managed entities. If you modify a field on a managed entity within a transaction, JPA automatically generates and executes an UPDATE statement when the transaction commits — **no need to call `save()` or `update()` explicitly**.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Persistence context = first-level cache = in-transaction entity store
- Scoped to one transaction (usually) or EntityManager
- **Dirty checking**: automatic UPDATE when managed entity is modified
- Entity states: New, Managed, Detached, Removed
- `flush()`: sync context to DB within transaction
- `clear()`: detach all entities from context
- Managed → Detached when transaction ends or `em.detach(entity)` called

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The persistence context is like an in-memory workspace for JPA within a transaction. Every entity you load within a transaction is tracked in this context. If you load the same entity twice, JPA recognizes it's already in the context and returns the same Java object without a second database hit. The most important feature is dirty checking — if you modify a field on an entity that's in the persistence context, JPA automatically detects that change and generates an UPDATE statement when the transaction commits. You don't need to call `save()` or `update()` — JPA handles it. This is different from Spring Data JPA where calling `save()` on an existing entity is the convention, but under the hood it's the same mechanism.

sections.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with Hibernate and PostgreSQL
sections.hook: The persistence context is why you can change a field on an entity and never call save — JPA already noticed.

beats.heading: What it is
beats.body: The persistence context is JPA's in-memory workspace for a transaction. Every entity you load or persist within a transaction lives in this context and is tracked. Think of it as a shopping basket — JPA keeps watching everything in the basket until you check out, which is when the transaction commits.

beats.heading: Two things it does
items: First-level cache: load the same entity twice by ID and JPA returns the same Java object — no second database query.
Dirty checking: modify a field on a managed entity and JPA generates an UPDATE automatically at commit time.

beats.heading: Lifetime
beats.body: The context is scoped to one transaction by default. When the transaction ends, managed entities become detached — JPA stops watching them. Changes after that point are not automatically persisted.

beats.heading: Production trap
beats.body: production trap: if you load a list of entities, modify them all in a loop, and the transaction commits, JPA fires an UPDATE per entity. Load 10,000 rows and modify them? That's 10,000 individual UPDATEs. For bulk changes, use a JPQL UPDATE or native SQL instead of looping over managed entities.

sections.cap: The persistence context is the first-level cache and the dirty-checking engine. Scoped to a transaction, it tracks every entity you touch and flushes changes automatically at commit.
followup_handoff: The natural follow-up is the four entity states — New, Managed, Detached, Removed.
They might ask the difference between the first-level cache and the second-level cache, which is shared across sessions.

followup_questions: What is dirty checking in JPA?
What are the four entity states in JPA?
What is the difference between first-level and second-level cache in JPA?

question: What are the four entity states in JPA?
title: JPA Entity States: New, Managed, Detached, Removed
direct_answer: JPA entities have four states: **New/Transient** (created with `new`, not in persistence context), **Managed** (in persistence context, changes auto-synced), **Detached** (was managed, now outside persistence context), **Removed** (marked for deletion). Each state determines what JPA does with the entity.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the difference between detached and removed states
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the practical implication of each state for CRUD operations

sections.title: Entity State Transitions
sections.content:
```
New/Transient: User u = new User(); // not in persistence context
    ↓ em.persist(u)
Managed: entity in persistence context, tracked for changes
    ↓ transaction ends / em.detach(u)
Detached: entity exists but not tracked, must merge() to update
    ↓ em.merge(u)
Managed again
    ↓ em.remove(u)
Removed: scheduled for DELETE on flush/commit
```

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **New/Transient**: `new Entity()` — no ID, not in DB, not in context
- **Managed**: loaded by `find()` or persisted — changes automatically flushed
- **Detached**: transaction ended — changes NOT automatically tracked
- **Removed**: `em.remove(entity)` — DELETE on next flush
- `merge(detachedEntity)` → returns a new managed instance
- Spring Data `save()`: calls `persist()` if new (no ID), `merge()` if detached (has ID)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: JPA entities go through four states. A `new` entity you created with `new User()` is in the New state — it's not tracked by JPA and not in the database. When you call `persist()` or load it from the database, it becomes Managed — JPA tracks all changes and automatically syncs to the database. When the transaction ends, managed entities become Detached — they exist in memory but JPA is no longer tracking them, so modifications won't be persisted automatically. To update a detached entity, you need to call `merge()`. Finally, Removed is when you've called `remove()` — the entity will be deleted from the database on the next flush. Understanding these states explains why `save()` in Spring Data JPA calls `persist()` for new entities but `merge()` for existing ones.

sections.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with Hibernate and PostgreSQL
sections.hook: Every JPA entity is always in one of four states, and that state decides whether JPA will save your changes or silently ignore them.

beats.heading: The four states
items: New — created with new User(), not in the database, not tracked by JPA.
Managed — loaded from the database or just persisted. JPA is watching it and will flush changes at commit.
Detached — was managed, but the transaction ended. Changes are no longer tracked automatically.
Removed — remove() was called. JPA will DELETE it from the database on the next flush.

beats.heading: How transitions happen
beats.body: You move from New to Managed by calling persist() or loading via find(). You move from Managed to Detached when the transaction closes. You can re-attach a detached entity by calling merge(), which returns a new managed copy. Calling remove() on a managed entity puts it in the Removed state.

beats.heading: Why Spring Data save() does two things
beats.body: Spring Data JPA's save() method checks if the entity has an ID. No ID means it's New, so save() calls persist(). Has an ID means it might be Detached, so save() calls merge(). This is why the same save() method works for both inserts and updates.

beats.heading: Sharp edge
beats.body: sharp edge: Detached is not the same as Removed. A detached entity still exists in the database — JPA just isn't tracking it anymore. A removed entity is scheduled to be deleted. Modifying a detached entity and expecting it to save is a very common bug in JPA code.

sections.cap: State determines behavior. Managed means JPA watches and saves. Detached means JPA has stepped away. Call merge() to bring a detached entity back under JPA's watch.
followup_handoff: They'll often ask the difference between persist() and merge() directly after this.
A related question is what happens to managed entities when a transaction rolls back — they're still in memory but the DB change is undone.

followup_questions: What is the difference between persist() and merge()?
What happens when a transaction ends to managed entities?
How does Spring Data's save() decide between persist() and merge()?
